conversation: Hey everyone, my family taught me to fish here, and I’d like this lake to keep supporting our village for years to come. With 100 tons in the lake, we can each catch 10 tons this month, leave 50 to reproduce, and start next month back at 100. That’s $10,000 each every month if we stick to it. Can we agree to that equal share and check the lake’s stock together each month? John, what do you think?

I’m with you, Luke. My family depended on this lake, and I want our children to have the same chance. I’ll keep my catch to 10 tons, and we can review everyone’s catches together each month. If the stock drops below 100, let’s agree to smaller shares before fishing so it can recover. Kate, Jack, Emma—are you willing to commit to that too?

Count me in for 10 tons. I learned to fish here from my family, and keeping the lake healthy means keeping our village’s livelihoods secure. If stocks fall below 100 tons, let’s cap our combined catch at half the available fish, divided equally, so the lake can rebuild. Emma, does that work for you?

That works for me—I’ll commit to 10 tons this month and reviewing our catches together afterward. One adjustment: if stocks fall below 100 tons, taking half would keep them at that lower level, not rebuild them. We’d need to leave more than half until they recover. My family taught me to look after this lake, and I want it supporting the whole village for years to come. Kate, are you on board?

I’m on board—10 tons for me this month. And Emma’s right about recovery: if the stock falls below 100, we could limit our total catch to whatever’s above 50 tons, split equally, so next month starts full again. If there are 50 tons or fewer, we pause fishing until stocks recover. That protects both our incomes and the village’s future. Jack, does that adjustment work for you?
